whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should take the B2C Commerce Developer exam?

personas.label: B2C Commerce developers
personas.description: You build storefront features with SFRA, ISML, and server-side JavaScript, and want to show your end-to-end development skills.

personas.label: Commerce engineers
personas.description: You work with controllers, templates, commerce APIs, and Business Manager settings across the B2C Commerce stack.

personas.label: Technical leads
personas.description: You guide cartridge structure, code releases, and storefront performance, and want to validate your technical experience.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the B2C Commerce Developer exam?
examDifficulty.summary: This exam covers a wide range of B2C Commerce development work. The 65% passing score is one part of the challenge; you also need to understand SFRA, templates, scripting, APIs, data, and Business Manager. Hands-on experience helps connect these topics.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
65% to pass, which is 39 correct answers out of 60.
Several development layers: questions can cover controllers, ISML templates, browser code, APIs, data, and Business Manager tasks.
Practice in a sandbox: Build an SFRA controller, extend a template, and try an OCAPI or SCAPI integration to prepare.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Use a B2C Commerce sandbox to build a custom controller, extend an SFRA template, and configure a job in Business Manager. Practice explaining why each pattern fits the task.

examFormat.heading: B2C Commerce Developer exam format
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test center. Questions cover practical development choices across the platform.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Some questions describe a storefront change and ask which SFRA pattern, controller approach, or API fits. Review cartridge path order, template overrides, and OCAPI resource settings.
bestWayToPass: Understand cartridge overrides: Learn how the path selects controllers and templates, and when `server.extend` or `server.replace` is appropriate.
Build with SFRA: Practice writing controllers, extending ISML templates, and using the `dw.*` APIs in a sandbox.
Compare the commerce APIs: Know the Shop and Data APIs, authentication basics for headless work, and when each API is useful.
Practice Business Manager tasks: Configure site preferences and jobs, manage code versions, and use logs and the pipeline profiler to investigate issues.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers full-stack SFCC development: SFRA cartridge architecture, ISML templates, controller scripting, OCAPI/SCAPI integration, and Business Manager configuration. The exam is 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, with a 65% pass mark, weighted towards Application Development (53%) and Data Management Using Business Manager Usage (24%).

keyConcepts.h2: B2C Commerce Developer exam: key concepts

blocks.heading: SFRA Architecture: Cartridges & Overrides
blocks.body: **SFRA** is Salesforce B2C Commerce’s reference storefront architecture. It uses **cartridges**, which package controllers, templates, models, and static files. The cartridge path in **Business Manager** sets priority: a cartridge earlier in the path wins when files share a location. To customize the storefront, put changes in your own cartridge and leave the base cartridge intact. In controllers, `server.extend` adds behavior to a route, while `server.replace` replaces it. Understand how path order affects which version runs.

blocks.heading: Controllers, Scripts & Server-Side Logic
blocks.body: SFRA controllers are JavaScript modules that use the `server` framework. Routes handle requests such as GET and POST, then render a template or return JSON. Middleware can add checks such as authentication, CSRF protection, or consent handling. Keep reusable business logic in models, helpers, or script modules instead of repeating it in controllers. The `dw.*` APIs provide access to server-side Commerce features. Custom scripts in `cartridge/scripts/` can hold logic shared by several routes. Be mindful of platform limits when a script queries or processes data.

blocks.heading: Templates (ISML) & Client-Side Assets
blocks.body: **ISML** is the server-side language used to build storefront pages. `<isinclude>` inserts another template, `<isloop>` repeats content for a collection, `<isset>` assigns a value, and `<isif>` handles a condition. Resource bundles store text for different locales. Put static JavaScript, CSS, and images in `cartridge/static/` and reference them with `URLUtils.staticURL()`. SFRA uses build tools such as Webpack to prepare browser code and SASS to produce CSS. Controllers pass data to templates through `pdict`. Keep dynamic content and caching behavior in mind when extending a page.

blocks.heading: Jobs, Feeds & Business Manager Configuration
blocks.body: Commerce Cloud jobs run scripts on a schedule or when started by an administrator. Teams use them for tasks such as importing product or inventory feeds and exporting orders. Configure job steps in **Business Manager**. **IMPEX** supports bulk import and export using formats such as XML and CSV. **Site Preferences** hold settings that administrators can change and code can read through `dw.system.Site.current.preferences`. **Custom Attributes** add fields to standard objects such as products, orders, or customers. Know where to configure a job and how a controller reads a site preference.

blocks.heading: Testing, Debugging & Deployment
blocks.body: Teams use build tools such as `sgmf-scripts` and deployment tools such as `sfcc-ci` to prepare and upload cartridges. Uploaded code is assigned to a code version, which is then activated. Use the Request Log and `dw.system.Logger` to investigate requests and application behavior. The Pipeline Profiler can help identify slow routes. Test controllers with dependencies that can be mocked, and use the project’s test tools and reports. For a release, understand the steps from uploading cartridges to activating the code version, and know where to look when errors appear in **Business Manager**.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the B2C Commerce Developer exam
scenarioTips.intro: The exam checks whether you can build and troubleshoot B2C Commerce storefront features. Practice tracing a request through a controller, template, script, and any API or Business Manager settings it depends on.

blocks.heading: SFRA Structure
blocks.body: Know how controllers, models, and ISML templates work together, and how the cartridge path chooses which implementation runs.

blocks.heading: Controller Routes
blocks.body: Practice creating and extending routes with `server.get`, `server.post`, `server.append`, `server.prepend`, and `server.replace`. Add middleware for the needed checks and return either JSON or a rendered template.

blocks.heading: ISML Templates
blocks.body: Review tags such as `<isset>`, `<isif>`, `<isloop>`, and `<isinclude>`. Learn how templates use locale, currency, and content assets, and how caching affects dynamic page content.

blocks.heading: Scripts and Commerce APIs
blocks.body: Write reusable CommonJS modules and use the `dw.*` APIs for catalog, order, and customer tasks. Know how server-side scripts call external services through `dw.net.HTTPClient`.

blocks.heading: Business Manager Settings
blocks.body: Practice setting up catalogs, price books, promotions, and site preferences. Know how Business Manager settings relate to the storefront and how to manage cartridges with the tools used by your team.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Certifications After Developer
nextCertsAfter.intro: After this certification, common next steps in the developer track:

sampleQuestions.question: A storefront needs to display an extra field for each product. Where should a developer define it?
options: Add a custom attribute to the product system object metadata
Create a separate custom object for product fields
Add the value to the site preference settings
Put the value directly in the template without extending product data
sampleQuestions.explanation: A custom attribute extends the standard product object so the additional value can be stored with each product.
whyWrong: A separate custom object is unnecessary when the field belongs to each product.
Site preferences store site-level settings, not individual product values.
A template can display data but does not define or store the product field.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the cartridge path determine?
options: Which payment providers are active
The order in which scheduled jobs run
Earlier matching cartridge wins
Which catalogs are assigned to the site
sampleQuestions.explanation: The path is searched in order, so a matching file in an earlier cartridge takes precedence over one later in the path.
whyWrong: Payment provider setup is separate from cartridge path order.
The path does not set job schedules.
Catalog assignment is configured separately in Business Manager.

sampleQuestions.question: A developer needs to change checkout behavior without editing base code. What should they do?
options: Use an earlier custom cartridge
Copy and rename the entire base cartridge
Remove the base cartridge and rebuild checkout
Edit the base cartridge and document the changes
sampleQuestions.explanation: A custom cartridge earlier in the path can override selected behavior while leaving the base cartridge available for upgrades.
whyWrong: Copying the whole base creates unnecessary maintenance work and diverges from the extension pattern.
Removing the base cartridge may remove standard features that the storefront depends on.
Direct edits to base code are hard to maintain through upgrades.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the main job of a storefront controller?
options: Store product data for storefront pages
Handle a request and decide what response to return
Schedule nightly catalog imports
Set the visual style for storefront pages
sampleQuestions.explanation: A controller handles the request, runs server-side logic, and chooses a template or response such as JSON.
whyWrong: Product data belongs to the catalog and data layer, not in the controller itself.
Jobs are configured separately and are not the controller’s main role.
Visual styling is handled by client-side assets such as CSS.

sampleQuestions.question: Two controllers need to use the same server-side logic. What is a good way to share it?
options: A shared script module
Create a template fragment for each controller to render
Copy the function into both controllers
Store the logic text in a custom object
sampleQuestions.explanation: A shared script module keeps one implementation that both controllers can call.
whyWrong: A template fragment is for rendering page content, not sharing server-side business logic.
Copying the function creates two versions that can drift apart.
A custom object stores data, not executable shared code.

sampleQuestions.question: Why should developers watch platform API and query quotas?
options: They limit how many products a catalog can contain
They control how often storefront cache can be cleared
Exceeding a limit can slow down or fail a request
They set the maximum number of cartridges on a site
sampleQuestions.explanation: The platform limits some operations within a request; exceeding those limits can produce warnings and cause failures.
whyWrong: Catalog size is not what these per-request limits describe.
Cache clearing frequency is controlled separately.
The limits do not determine how many cartridges a site can use.

sampleQuestions.question: What do OCAPI and SCAPI provide in a B2C Commerce solution?
options: A way to import a catalog from a retailer’s backend only
The rendering engine for shopper-facing pages
The screens merchants use in Business Manager
Commerce APIs for external clients
sampleQuestions.explanation: These APIs let external applications, including headless storefronts and integrations, work with commerce data and operations.
whyWrong: Catalog imports can use other supported feed and job patterns; that is not the APIs’ only purpose.
Storefront page rendering is handled by the storefront architecture or a separate front end.
Business Manager provides merchant configuration screens.

sampleQuestions.question: A loyalty program offers members a different product price. Which setup supports this?
options: Duplicate all eligible products in another catalog
Assign a separate price book to the member customer group
Require each member to enter a promotion code
Store the member price in a custom product attribute
sampleQuestions.explanation: A customer group can be associated with a price book so eligible shoppers receive the group’s prices.
whyWrong: Duplicating products is not needed to provide group-specific prices.
A promotion code is not the same as resolving prices through a customer group.
A custom attribute does not replace the platform’s price book behavior.

sampleQuestions.question: A job must process the full product catalog. What should the developer plan for?
options: Turn off the storefront for the whole run
Process the job in chunks
Handle records one at a time in a single long operation
Run the job during peak traffic to spot errors quickly
sampleQuestions.explanation: Breaking large workloads into chunks helps the job stay within limits and recover if a step fails.
whyWrong: The storefront does not generally need to be disabled for a catalog job.
One long operation can consume too many resources and fail before completion.
Peak traffic is a poor time to run a resource-intensive job.

sampleQuestions.question: Why does storefront caching matter?
options: It guarantees the catalog is always current
It lowers response time under load
It removes the need to consider API quotas
It guarantees every shopper sees personalized prices
sampleQuestions.explanation: Caching suitable content lets the storefront serve pages faster under real traffic.
whyWrong: Caching can make content stale unless its rules and invalidation are managed.
Caching does not remove platform limits on API or query use.
Personalized pricing still needs correct shopper and cache handling.

sampleQuestions.question: Personalized content for one shopper appears in another shopper’s cached page. What is the likely cause?
options: A platform quota was exceeded while rendering the page
A product is missing a custom attribute
Cache personalized output by shopper
The custom cartridge is in the wrong path position
sampleQuestions.explanation: If a cached response depends on the shopper but the cache does not distinguish shoppers, one person may receive another person’s content.
whyWrong: A quota issue may affect request behavior but does not explain sharing one shopper’s cached output.
A product field issue would not make personalized output cross between shoppers.
Cartridge order affects which code runs, not whether the cache varies by shopper.

sampleQuestions.question: How does a storefront catalog differ from a master catalog?
options: One is for merchant edits and one is only for developer edits
One contains physical goods and the other only digital goods
One is for a site and the other is for a locale
Master defines products; storefront organizes browsing
sampleQuestions.explanation: Products are defined in the master catalog and placed into storefront catalog structures that control site navigation.
whyWrong: Both catalog types can be managed through appropriate commerce tools and permissions.
The difference is not based on whether products are physical or digital.
A storefront catalog controls the assortment and navigation; it is not simply a locale setting.

sampleQuestions.question: A retailer switches to a headless front end that calls B2C Commerce APIs. What changes for the developer?
options: Jobs can no longer run without a storefront
The cartridge path has no use anywhere in the solution
System objects can no longer have custom attributes
The front end renders; Commerce serves API data
sampleQuestions.explanation: In a headless design, a separate front end handles presentation and consumes platform data and operations through APIs.
whyWrong: Jobs can still run as platform processes in a headless implementation.
The cartridge path can still matter for server-side code and other platform features.
Custom attributes can still extend system objects in a headless solution.

sampleQuestions.question: A custom checkout needs to collect payment details. What is the safer approach?
options: Let the payment provider collect the details directly
Send card details through the controller and log them for later
Save card details in a custom shopper attribute
Keep card details in the session until the order is placed
sampleQuestions.explanation: Use the provider’s hosted fields or redirect so raw card data does not pass through the storefront application or its logs.
whyWrong: Logging card details exposes sensitive data and should be avoided.
Storing card details on the shopper profile would retain sensitive payment data in the application.
Session storage still puts card data in the application environment.

sampleQuestions.question: Which work is a B2C Commerce developer mainly responsible for?
options: Choosing the storefront’s visual design and brand style
Deciding which products the merchandising team should promote
Storefront behavior, integrations, and data extensions
Operating the underlying hosting infrastructure
sampleQuestions.explanation: Developers implement and customize storefront behavior, extend the data model, and connect Commerce with other systems.
whyWrong: Visual design may be delivered with developers, but this does not describe the developer’s main platform responsibility.
Merchandising teams decide which products to feature.
Salesforce operates the underlying Commerce hosting infrastructure.
